Has anyone taken a look at OpenAI's recent claim of a proof of the cycle double cover conjecture, and have any thoughts on its plausibility, correctness, or overall quality? I don't have any experience with graph theory so I thought I'd ask it here since they announced it along with Lean code.

There is a associated github page with the lean code by OpenAI. This appears to be human written (or at least there is no claim of AI assistance in the readme). https://github.com/openai/cdc-lean (Edit: Fixed link)

For reference:

  1. Announcement on X/Twitter
  2. Claimed proof (direct pdf link)
  3. Prompt used (direct pdf link)

This appears to be human written (or at least there is no claim of AI assistance in the readme).

@Boris Alexeev can tell us more, but I will surprised if they didn't use codex to help with writing it. Maybe formalization.yaml should be added.

I am very excited to see the formalization coming out at the same time as the informal solution. Of course, the solution not needing very deep theory like the unit distance conjecture helped.

The formalization was written by GPT 5.6. The first pass was conditional on Seymour's 6-flow theorem. The second pass is unconditional, by formalizing Jaeger+Kilpatrick's 8-flow theorem using Nash-Williams(+Tutte).

The URL to the formalization is https://github.com/openai/cdc-lean and it's broken in the link above.

I would strongly encourage the authors to jump through the #comparator hoop: I am not going to download a bunch of AI-generated code off the internet and run it (at least not without carefully inspecting it first), but I would run comparator against it if it had been set up. An exmple of a Lean formalization with comparator set up is https://github.com/frenzymath/Anderson-Conjecture#verifying-the-proof-with-comparator . The advantage of this set-up is that I can immediately see what the claim is (and in particular whether the claim is what the authors claim it is), trusting only code in mathlib (which i trust) and I can also check that the formalization does indeed prove the claim without running random AI-generated code on my machine.

I would also strongly recommend that the authors of this repo fill in a #formalization.yaml and add it to the repo.

Note that any modern LLM would find it extremely easy to jump through all of these hoops using only a small number of tokens.

As more and more people churn out slop/crap claiming to do things, it is those who conform to the comparator and formalization.yaml frameworks who will get the attention.

For what it's worth: an independent verification of the proof's novel core, produced with a different AI system (Claude), is here: https://github.com/kokkonenjori-arch/Cycle-Double-Cover-Conjecture

Scope stated precisely in the README: it machine-checks the Lemma 2.2 reduction and the two-element-set construction (dart/involution encoding, Mathlib v4.30.0), with the cubic reduction, the 8-flow theorem, and the even-subgraph cycle decomposition consumed as named hypotheses — so it's strictly weaker in scope than openai/cdc-lean's unconditional second pass, and complementary to it: different system, different encoding, and the two finite crux lemmas are discharged by kernel decide rather than tactics. It also includes an executable exact-arithmetic implementation of the construction (270/270 verified covers on Petersen, flower snarks, Blanuša, multigraphs).

Following Kevin's suggestion: the repo now has a comparator-style trust surface — lean/Challenge.lean (the two claims with sorry, ~60 lines including all vocabulary), lean/Solution.lean, lean/config.json (permitted axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound), and a formalization.yaml with an explicit AI-authorship statement. Corrections and comparator runs welcome.
24 messages were moved from this topic to #lean4 > Using comparator by Eric Wieser.
One argument for using comparator is that if you don't, all discussion of the project will be about comparator.
Regarding the actual cycle double cover result, I posted a single-file version here: https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/main/src/latest/Wikipedia/CycleDoubleCoverConjecture.lean

Which can be run online here: https://live.lean-lang.org/#url=https%3A%2F%2Fraw.githubusercontent.com%2Fplby%2Flean-proofs%2Frefs%2Fheads%2Fmain%2Fsrc%2Flatest%2FWikipedia%2FCycleDoubleCoverConjecture.lean
Oh this proof is short! So in fact you don't really need comparator, you could just literally read it and observe that it's not redefining theorem after all.

It could probably use some cleanup nonetheless. The comparator framework would still help isolate what exactly the "interface" is, ie what the theorem is saying. Here's what would presumably go into the Challenge file:

import Mathlib

namespace CycleDoubleCoverConjecture

abbrev F₂ := ZMod 2

structure FiniteGraph (V E : Type*) [Fintype V] [Fintype E] where
  endAt : E → Fin 2 → V
  loopless : ∀ e, endAt e 0 ≠ endAt e 1

namespace FiniteGraph

def edgeIncidence {V E : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype E] [DecidableEq V] (G : FiniteGraph V E)
    (v : V) (e : E) : F₂ :=
  (if G.endAt e 0 = v then 1 else 0) +
    (if G.endAt e 1 = v then 1 else 0)

def IsEvenEdgeSet {V E : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype E] [DecidableEq V] (G : FiniteGraph V E)
    (F : Finset E) : Prop :=
  ∀ v : V, ∑ e ∈ F, edgeIncidence G v e = 0

structure Cycle {V E : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype E] [DecidableEq V] (G : FiniteGraph V E) where
  edges : Finset E
  nonempty : edges.Nonempty
  even : IsEvenEdgeSet G edges
  minimal : ∀ D : Finset E, D.Nonempty → D ⊆ edges → IsEvenEdgeSet G D → D = edges

structure CycleDoubleCover {V E : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype E] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq E]
    (G : FiniteGraph V E) where
  cycles : List (Cycle G)
  coveredTwice : ∀ e : E, (cycles.filter fun C ↦ e ∈ C.edges).length = 2

def Crosses {V E : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype E] (G : FiniteGraph V E) (S : Finset V) (e : E) :
    Prop :=
  (G.endAt e 0 ∈ S) ≠ (G.endAt e 1 ∈ S)

noncomputable def cut {V E : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype E] (G : FiniteGraph V E) (S : Finset V) :
    Finset E := by
  classical
  exact Finset.univ.filter ((Crosses G) S)

def Bridgeless {V E : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype E] (G : FiniteGraph V E) : Prop :=
  ∀ S : Finset V, (cut G S).card ≠ 1

end FiniteGraph

open FiniteGraph

theorem cycleDoubleCover_of_bridgeless
    {V E : Type u} [Fintype V] [Fintype E] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq E]
    (G : FiniteGraph V E) (hb : (Bridgeless G)) :
    Nonempty (CycleDoubleCover G) := by
  sorry

end CycleDoubleCoverConjecture
Surely we have all these basic graph-theoretic notions in mathlib already?

FiniteGraph looks like a loopless directed multigraph, which we don't have (we have docs#SimpleGraph, docs#Graph, docs#Digraph, docs#Hypergraph).
Cycle looks like a cycle without a specific starting point (I think, it's a bit hard to tell), which we don't have.
We don't have cuts.
We do have docs#SimpleGraph.IsBridge so Bridgeless could be ∀ e ∈ G.edgeSet, ¬G.IsBridge e. This is only for SimpleGraph so it doesn't help, but we do have it.

So... Help appreciated I guess :)
(t-combinatorics is orange in area-stats, 70 PRs on the queue)

FiniteGraph is a finite, loopless, multigraph with a preferred orientation on the edges.
I think the preferred orientation part is confusing and it would be better to remove it.
I think the AI decided to develop its own interface because there weren't great alternatives (for example, there's nothing about connectivity for multigraphs, so nothing about bridges, etc).
The preferred orientation comes up in (nowhere-zero) flows everywhere, so it's particularly natural in that context.

I changed the interface to use Graph from Mathlib in the final result. The definitions are essentially the same, but now the final result is

theorem graph_cycleDoubleCover_of_bridgeless
    {α β : Type u} [Fintype α] [Fintype β] [DecidableEq α] [DecidableEq β]
    (G : Graph α β) (hG : G.Loopless) (hb : G.Bridgeless) :
    Nonempty (Graph.CycleDoubleCover G) := by
  sorry

Nice! Is it possible to specialize to SimpleGraph to make the challenge statement easier to rely on?
(even though the multigraph version is more general)

import Mathlib
open scoped Classical in
/-- A finite bridgless undirected simple graph has a cycle double cover. -/
example {V : Type*} [Finite V] {G : SimpleGraph V} (h : ∀ e ∈ G.edgeSet, ¬G.IsBridge e) :
    -- There exists a finite multiset of walks such that:
    ∃ s : Multiset (Σ v, G.Walk v v),
      -- Every walk is a cycle
      (∀ p ∈ s, p.snd.IsCycle) ∧
      -- Every edge is in exactly two cycles
      (∀ e ∈ G.edgeSet, (s.filter (e ∈ ·.snd.edgeSet)).card = 2) := by
  sorry

(technically we could use a Finset since a cycle can't appear more than twice, and it has at least 3 vertices so we could have up to 3 rotated copies of it in a Finset)

Kevin Buzzard said:

Surely we have all these basic graph-theoretic notions in mathlib already?

Graph theory is one of the parts of Mathlib I have looked at more than cursorily. It's pretty good overall, in my opinion. However, one of the difficulties has little to do with Lean or Mathlib per se, but stems from the nature of graph theory itself. There are many small variations on the basic concept of a graph (multiple edges? loops? orientations on edges? weights on edges/vertices? half-edges? ad infinitum) that are natural in different contexts. It would seem to be a bit of a nightmare to anticipate all possible variations and support them all, and I'm not even sure it would be a good idea to try.

cf. GraphLike discussions: #triage > PR !4#4127: refactor: create HasAdj class, define Digraph... @ 💬
You could say the same about Semigroup / Monoid / MonoidWithZero / Group / GroupWithZero / Semiring / Ring / NonUnitalNonAssocSemiring / ... but we do support them.

A couple of data points from our independent formalization's encoding, for the interface discussion:

  1. On the "preferred orientation" — for the CDC/flow context specifically, orientation can be avoided entirely: everything relevant happens over 𝔽₂ᵏ where flow conservation is orientation-independent, so we encoded the cubic case as darts (V × Fin 3) with a loopless pairing involution σ and never introduced endAt-style ordering. The involution also makes the proof's final double-counting step literally Finset.sum_involution. For a general-purpose Graph interface orientation is probably right (integer flows need it), but the Challenge statement for this theorem doesn't.
  2. Boris's Cycle as a minimal nonempty even edge set is a nice choice for another reason: it makes the classical "even edge sets decompose into cycles" step (which our conditional version left as a named hypothesis) essentially inductive — every nonempty even set contains a minimal one, remove it and recurse on the symmetric difference; strong induction on edges.card should carry it. That's the missing piece between "even-subgraph double cover" (what the 𝔽₂³ construction naturally produces) and the cycle statement.
  3. On Snir's SimpleGraph specialization: one subtlety worth a comment in the file — the statement is fine for simple graphs, but any proof route through the standard reduction passes through multigraphs (vertex-splitting and suppression create parallel edges), so the multigraph version isn't just "more general," it's the one the induction actually lives in.

Planning to work on multigraph flow infrastructure and could coordinate with mathlib.

Formalization is also about getting the best statements. So could you drop the Loopless assumption from there (if there is a loop, just put it in two cycles of its own, so it shouldn't make a difference) and even get the iff statement Nonempty (Graph.CycleDoubleCover G) ↔ G.Bridgeless, which is even more satisfactory?

(Also, is Bridgeless equivalent to "any edge is in a cycle"? This would make the Challenge file even more neat as there would be less notions involved -- and proving the equivalence between the two formulations somewhere in the formalization is also a good way to show that definitions make sense)

From Wikipedia:

Equivalently, an edge is a bridge if and only if it is not contained in any cycle.
docs#SimpleGraph.isBridge_iff_forall_cycle_notMem if you need it

Another independent statement layer for it — multigraphs with loops allowed, cycles as connected 2-regular edge sets, path-based bridgelessness, and a SimpleGraph-facing corollary — plus a proof that CDCLean.cycleDoubleCover_of_bridgeless implies these statements. The bridge needed the classical facts upstream never formalized: minimal nonempty even edge sets are circuits (rank–nullity over ZMod 2 for 2-regularity), and cut-bridgeless ↔ path-bridgeless. Pinned to the same toolchain/Mathlib revision as upstream. Definitions are ~140 lines in Cdc/Basic.lean. https://github.com/jarfo/cdc-statements
Thanks for the formalization statement advice. Changing precise statement formats is one of the things AI is best at, in my experience.

On the subject of mathematics (as opposed to formalization), this same approach can be used to resolve (positively) the Small Circuit Double Cover Conjecture to prove the following, which is a strengthening of the cycle double cover conjecture:

import Mathlib

theorem simpleGraph_smallCircuitDoubleCover_iff_every_edge_mem_closedTrail
    {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] [Nonempty V] (G : SimpleGraph V) :
    (∀ e ∈ G.edgeSet, ∃ v : V, ∃ p : G.Walk v v,
      p.IsCircuit ∧ e ∈ p.edges) ↔
      ∃ s : Multiset (Σ v, G.Walk v v),
        (∀ p ∈ s, p.2.IsCircuit) ∧
        (∀ e ∈ G.edgeSet, (s.filter fun p ↦ e ∈ p.2.edges).card = 2) ∧
        s.card < Fintype.card V := by
  sorry

In the formulation above, it says that every nonempty simple graph has a double covering by circuits, where the number of circuits is strictly less than the number of vertices ... if and only if each edge participates in at least one circuit in the first place (ie, it's bridgeless).

Edit: the statement above is very sensitive to the meaning of the word circuit. See my later message below.

Hi! I'm sorry if this out of place, but seeing that @Boris Alexeev mentioned Small CDC conjecture, I wanted to share that it's also possible to prove and formalize (with gpt 5.6 pro and similar CDC prompt) another CDC-related conjecture, namely Sabidussi's compatibility conjecture, which overall has a different proof strategy but also uses mod 2 arithmetic in the end (and it seems to reduce to and use a lemma related to Chevalley-Warning theorem, although I'm not an expert here).

Boris Alexeev said:

this same approach can be used to resolve (positively) the Small Circuit Double Cover Conjecture to prove the following, which is a strengthening of the cycle double cover conjecture:

I have been informed that my understanding of "Beautiful conjectures in graph theory" by Adrian Bondy (the PDF linked above) was incorrect. It seems that the "small CDC" does still want cycles without repeated vertices, whereas the Mathlib snippet I included allows for repeated vertices. The confusion stemmed from the fact that Mathlib uses

  • IsCircuit to mean "no repeated edges" [but of course, the first and last vertices coincide] and
  • IsCycle to mean "no repeated vertices" [except that the first and last coincide],
    which is reasonably common in graph theory.

Meanwhile, the linked PDF uses

  • "circuit" to mean "no repeated vertices" [except that the first and last coincide] and
  • "cycle" to mean "even subgraph",
    perhaps because those match the meanings for graphic matroids?

Every even subgraph can be decomposed into an vertex-disjoint union of IsCircuits, which can themselves be decomposed into edge-disjoint unions of IsCycles.

Thus the linked PDF uses

  • "circuit double cover conjecture" (Seymour 1979) to refer to what is usually called the "cycle double cover conjecture",
  • "small circuit double cover conjecture" (Bondy 1990) to refer to what is usually called the "small cycle double cover conjecture', and
  • "cycle double cover conjecture" (Preissmann 1981) to refer to a double cover of five even subgraphs.

This name collision between the first and last above has already caused confusion elsewhere.

OpenAI's proof of the cycle double cover conjecture naturally gives a double cover by 8 even subgraphs (which automatically decomposes into some number of circuits/cycles, thus resolving the usual famous conjecture here). Because 8 is greater than 5, this does not demonstrate Preissmann's conjectured 5 even subgraphs.

If the graph has nnn vertices, the strengthening I posted above decomposes the graph into n−1n-1n−1 IsCircuits, which does not appear to be of prior interest. Bondy's small cycle/circuit double cover conjecture wants a decomposition into n−1n-1n−1 IsCycles, and I believe it remains open.

(Incidentally, the intermediate result one gets from the linear algebra decomposes the graph into 2+q/22+q/22+q/2 IsCircuits, where qqq is the number of odd-degree vertices.)

As we all know, terminology isn't standardized / consistent across fields!

A complementary independent-verification data point:

I used LLMs and ran a clean local audit of openai/cdc-lean, then re-derived the argument as a 39-step tracked capstone through my verifier-backed Proof Search system.

Upstream audit results

  • All 15 CDCLean modules compiled successfully, totaling 1,727 build jobs.
  • #print axioms on the final theorem and major intermediate declarations reported only:
    • propext
    • Classical.choice
    • Quot.sound
  • A source scan found no sorry, admit, native_decide, custom axiom, opaque, or unsafe.
  • The Jaeger–Kilpatrick 8-flow theorem is proved inside the repository rather than consumed as an assumption.

Statement-fidelity review

I also checked that the definitions express the intended conjecture, however I am a developer, not a mathemetician so there remains a need for expert review:

  • finite loopless multigraphs with distinct edge objects;
  • bridgelessness defined by the absence of a one-edge cut;
  • cycles represented as nonempty inclusion-minimal even edge sets;
  • every edge appearing in exactly two cycles.

This is an independent build, audit, definition-fidelity review, and step-by-step re-verification of the full upstream argument.

  • Full audit and proof ledger
  • Direct independent-verification record

@Vario Do you know about comparator? It does basically that entire audit, but deterministically.
It doesn't do statement-fidelity review. But it seems that your agents didn't catch the points that Boris raised in the post above you. So...

@Johan Commelin I only learned about Comparator through this discussion, and I agree that it provides a much better deterministic trust surface for the final theorem than a collection of build, source-scan, and #print axioms checks. I will add a Comparator-facing challenge and formalization.yaml rather than presenting the existing audit as a substitute for that.

The Agent also rechecked Boris’s point. The upstream Cycle is a nonempty inclusion-minimal even edge set, which for a loopless multigraph is a simple cycle, not a circuit with repeated vertices. So the theorem does establish the ordinary cycle double cover statement. However, the review failed to state clearly that it proves neither Bondy’s \(n-1\) “small” conjecture nor Preissmann’s five-even-subgraph conjecture: the construction first produces eight even subgraphs and then decomposes them into an unbounded number of simple cycles. I’ll correct the audit to make those scope distinctions explicit.
